content: 1. Best practices should be established to enhance patient literacy, empower both patients and communities, and redefine patient-centered care. This approach aims to reduce the emergence and transmission of drug-resistant viruses. 2. There is a lack of comprehensive reports that define the most sensitive, cost-effective, and actionable methods for HIV drug resistance (HIVDR) testing, as well as strategies for implementing these methods in lowand middle-income countries. 3. A standardized and simplified approach to managing data from next-generation sequencing outputs should be developed to facilitate its use in resource-limited settings. 4. A simplified, evidence-based tool should be created and validated to interpret clinically relevant drug resistance mutations. This tool should be designed for use at the point of care. 5. The feasibility of affordable, simple, public health-oriented tests that combine viral load and HIVDR testing should be explored. These tests should be adaptable to various specimen types, such as dried blood spots, dried plasma spots, and whole blood, and should be deployable at or near the point of care to support decentralization. 6. The potential of inexpensive and straightforward drug level tests should be investigated. These tests could be used at or near the point of care to guide decisions on whether HIVDR genotypic testing is necessary, particularly for quickly identifying individuals who are non-adherent to antiretroviral therapy (ART). 7. The prevalence of pretreatment HIV drug resistance (HIVDR) must be assessed within a broader context. A comprehensive and nationally representative evaluation of HIVDR and ART program performance is essential in all countries to minimize resistance. 8. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed a comprehensive framework to support this effort. This includes guidance on surveillance of acquired HIVDR in individuals experiencing ART failure, population-level viral load suppression assessments, and measurement of ART clinic and program factors predictive of HIVDR (early-warning indicators). 9. Preventing HIVDR remains a critical component of the global and national response to HIV. It is also a key strategic objective of WHO’s Global Action Plan on HIV Drug Resistance 2017–2021. 10. WHO-validated early-warning indicator tools should be used to monitor resistance drivers at the clinic level and measure program quality. This enables the identification of factors related to patient care, behavior, and clinicor program-level management, as well as addressing gaps in service delivery. 11. Annual monitoring of early-warning indicators of HIVDR provides insights into ART clinic and program performance. This includes adherence to ART, retention rates, viral load testing coverage, viral load suppression levels, frequency of antiretroviral drug stock-outs, and timely and appropriate switches to second-line ART when indicated. 12. Detailed definitions of each early-warning indicator are available in the 2017 WHO consolidated guidelines on person-centered HIV patient monitoring and case surveillance. 13. Public health actions to prevent HIVDR and address suboptimal performance of quality-of-care indicators are outlined in Web Annex 3. 14. The guidelines will be disseminated as printed publications and electronically on the WHO website in English and French. The web version will include all annexes, and a library of supporting documentation and evidence will also be made available. 15. WHO headquarters will collaborate with regional and country offices, as well as implementing partners, to ensure widespread dissemination of the guidelines through regional and subregional meetings. Assistance will be provided to Member States to adapt the guidelines to their national contexts. 16. An evaluation framework has been developed to assess the uptake of the guidelines and identify barriers to effective implementation. This policy analysis will evaluate the use and appropriateness of the new guidelines within the context of the 2016 WHO consolidated antiretroviral (ARV) guidelines. 17. The WHO Department of HIV and Global Hepatitis Programme plans to review the uptake of WHO’s HIV-related recommendations at regular intervals. Continued monitoring of viral load suppression and HIVDR prevalence at the population level will inform the impact on health outcomes. 18. WHO is committed to measuring, preventing, and mitigating the effects of HIVDR on treatment outcomes. This will be achieved through country support, surveillance protocols, and guidance on HIVDR prevention and program strengthening, which will be adapted as new evidence emerges. 19. The introduction of new ARV drugs in first-line ART is anticipated to influence the need and type of response required to address HIVDR. The choice of antiretroviral therapy in the context of pretreatment drug resistance will be considered in the next update of the 2016 WHO consolidated ARV guidelines, planned for 2019. 20. WHO strives to consolidate key resources to provide a centralized repository for program managers and policymakers. Supplements are developed and incorporated when new evidence necessitates guidance, ensuring the guidelines remain up-to-date. 21. WHO’s efforts to address HIVDR include surveillance, intervention effectiveness studies, and implementation research. These efforts aim to provide evidence-based recommendations to improve health outcomes and strengthen HIV programs globally.
